responses: In Scrum, there are three key roles: The Product Owner (maximizes product value), the Scrum Master (facilitates the process), and the Development Team (delivers the increment). Each role has distinct responsibilities that complement each other.

The Product Owner is responsible for managing the Product Backlog, ordering items to best achieve goals, and ensuring the Development Team understands items. They're the single authority on product decisions.
The Scrum Master serves the team by helping everyone understand Scrum theory, practices, and rules. They remove impediments, facilitate events when needed, and help the organization adopt Scrum.

Scrum has five events: Sprint (container for all other events), Sprint Planning (defines sprint work), Daily Scrum (15-min synchronization), Sprint Review (inspect increment), and Sprint Retrospective (process improvement).
Sprint Planning answers two questions: What can be done in this Sprint? How will the chosen work get done? The entire Scrum Team participates, and it's time-boxed to 8 hours for a one-month Sprint.
The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Development Team to synchronize activities and create a plan for the next 24 hours. It's held at the same time and place each day to reduce complexity.

Scrum's artifacts are: Product Backlog (ordered list of everything needed), Sprint Backlog (items selected for the Sprint plus delivery plan), and Increment (sum of all completed Product Backlog items).
The Product Backlog is a living artifact that evolves as the product and environment change. Items have attributes like description, order, estimate, and value. It's never complete.

The Definition of Done creates transparency by providing everyone a shared understanding of what it means for work to be complete. When an Increment is described as 'Done', everyone must understand what 'Done' means.

Scrum is founded on five values: Commitment (to achieving team goals), Courage (to do the right thing), Focus (on Sprint work), Openness (about work and challenges), and Respect (for each other as capable individuals).
These values guide the Scrum Team's decisions, actions, and behavior. When these values are embodied and lived by the Scrum Team, transparency, inspection, and adaptation come to life.
Success depends on people becoming more proficient in living these five values. The team reflects on how they're practicing the values and identifies ways to improve.

Scrum is founded on empirical process control theory, which asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is known. It uses an iterative, incremental approach to optimize predictability and control risk.

The three pillars upholding empirical process control are: Transparency (significant aspects must be visible), Inspection (frequently inspect artifacts), and Adaptation (adjust process when inspection reveals unacceptable variance).
Transparency requires those aspects be defined by a common standard so observers share a common understanding. This includes a common language and a shared Definition of Done.
The Product Owner is responsible for managing the Product Backlog, which includes clearly expressing items, ordering them, optimizing value, and ensuring visibility, transparency, and clarity.

Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items. It's an ongoing activity where the team adds detail, estimates, and order to items. No more than 10% of Development Team capacity.
Prioritization is based on value, risk, dependencies, and learning opportunities. The Product Owner uses techniques like MoSCoW, Cost of Delay, and Value vs Effort to make ordering decisions.
The Product Owner is the liaison between stakeholders and the Development Team. They must balance competing interests and make the best decisions for the product's success.
Effective stakeholder management involves regular communication, setting expectations, gathering feedback, and ensuring their needs are understood and represented in the Product Backlog.
The Sprint Review is a key event for stakeholder collaboration. The Product Owner discusses what's 'Done' and not 'Done,' and the group collaborates on what to do next.
The Product Owner is responsible for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Development Team. How this is done varies across organizations, teams, and individuals.

Value can be measured in many ways: revenue, cost reduction, customer satisfaction, market share, learning, risk reduction, or strategic alignment. The Product Owner must understand what value means for their context.
Focus on outcomes, not outputs. Delivering features is not the goal—achieving business and user outcomes is. Use metrics like OKRs, NPS, and business KPIs to measure value.
AWS (Amazon Web Services) is the world's most comprehensive cloud platform with over 200 services. Core services include EC2 (compute), S3 (storage), RDS (databases), and Lambda (serverless).
AWS operates on a pay-as-you-go model. You only pay for what you use, with no upfront costs or long-term contracts. This makes it cost-effective for startups to large enterprises.
AWS Regions are physical locations worldwide with multiple Availability Zones. Each AZ is isolated but connected through low-latency links for high availability and fault tolerance.
DevOps is a set of practices that combines software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) to shorten the development lifecycle and deliver high-quality software continuously.
CI/CD (Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment) automates the integration of code changes and deployment to production. This enables faster, more reliable releases with less manual effort.
Key DevOps practices include: infrastructure as code, continuous monitoring, automated testing, version control, and collaborative culture between development and operations teams.
Containers package code and dependencies together so applications run reliably across computing environments. Docker is the most popular containerization platform.
Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform that automates deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It's become the industry standard.
Benefits of containers include: consistent environments, faster deployment, better resource utilization, easier scaling, and simplified dependency management.

Machine Learning is a subset of AI where systems learn from data without explicit programming. Main types: Supervised Learning (labeled data), Unsupervised Learning (patterns in unlabeled data), and Reinforcement Learning (learning through rewards).
The ML workflow includes: data collection, preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection, training, evaluation, tuning, and deployment. Each step is crucial for model success.
Common ML algorithms include: Linear Regression, Decision Trees, Random Forests, Neural Networks, SVMs, and k-Nearest Neighbors. Choose based on your data and problem type.
Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT are neural networks trained on vast amounts of text data. They can understand and generate human-like text, making them powerful for various NLP tasks.
LLMs use transformer architecture with self-attention mechanisms to process text. They're pre-trained on general text, then fine-tuned for specific tasks or domains.
Key considerations when using LLMs: prompt engineering (crafting effective inputs), token limits, API costs, rate limits, privacy concerns, and potential biases in outputs.
Data Engineering builds and maintains the infrastructure for data generation, storage, and processing. It involves designing pipelines, managing databases, and ensuring data quality.
ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) processes move data from sources to destinations. Modern approaches include ELT (load before transform) and real-time streaming pipelines.
Tools in the data engineer's toolkit: Apache Spark (big data processing), Airflow (workflow orchestration), Kafka (streaming), dbt (transformation), and various database systems.

The CIA Triad is the foundation of information security: Confidentiality (data privacy), Integrity (data accuracy), and Availability (data accessibility). All security measures aim to maintain these three principles.
Defense in depth uses multiple layers of security controls. If one layer fails, others continue protecting. Layers include: physical, network, host, application, and data security.
The principle of least privilege means giving users only the minimum access they need. This limits damage from compromised accounts and reduces attack surface.

OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical web application security risks: Injection flaws, Broken Authentication, Sensitive Data Exposure, XXE, Broken Access Control, Security Misconfiguration, XSS, Insecure Deserialization, Components with Known Vulnerabilities, and Insufficient Logging.
SQL Injection occurs when attackers insert malicious SQL in input fields. Prevention: use parameterized queries, input validation, and ORM frameworks. Never concatenate user input into SQL strings.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) injects malicious scripts into web pages viewed by others. Prevention: sanitize user input, escape output, use Content Security Policy, and validate data on both client and server sides.
Encryption transforms data into unreadable format without the decryption key. Symmetric encryption uses the same key for encryption/decryption. Asymmetric uses public/private key pairs.

Hashing creates a fixed-size output from input data. It's one-way (can't reverse) and collision-resistant. Used for password storage, data integrity checks, and digital signatures. Common: SHA-256, bcrypt.

TLS/SSL secures internet communications. HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt HTTP traffic. Certificates verify server identity. Always use HTTPS for sensitive data and enable HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security).

Effective study strategies: 1) Space out your learning (spaced repetition), 2) Test yourself regularly, 3) Teach concepts to others, 4) Apply knowledge to real projects, 5) Take breaks and sleep well.
For certification exams: Understand concepts deeply, don't just memorize. Practice with sample questions. Focus on 'why' and 'how', not just 'what'. Create mind maps to connect ideas.
The academy's projects are designed to reinforce learning through practice. Don't skip them—hands-on experience helps concepts stick and prepares you for real-world applications.
Certifications demonstrate commitment and baseline knowledge, but they're not everything. Combine them with projects, networking, continuous learning, and soft skills for career success.

Tech career paths: Individual Contributor (senior engineer, architect), Management (team lead, engineering manager), or Specialist (security expert, data scientist). Choose based on your interests and strengths.
Continuous learning is essential in tech. Stay current with industry trends, contribute to open source, attend conferences, read technical blogs, and work on side projects to grow your skills.

There are 8 major AI model architectures: LLMs (Large Language Models), LCMs (Large Concept Models), VLMs (Vision-Language Models), SLMs (Small Language Models), MoE (Mixture of Experts), MLMs (Masked Language Models), LAMs (Large Action Models), and SAMs (Segment Anything Models). Each serves different tasks. LLMs are AI models, but not all AI models are LLMs.

Not all AI models are LLMs! The 8 main architectures are: 1) LLM — text generation, 2) LCM — concept-level multilingual reasoning, 3) VLM — image + text understanding, 4) SLM — lightweight edge inference, 5) MoE — efficient sparse expert routing, 6) MLM — bidirectional NLU, 7) LAM — autonomous task execution, 8) SAM — pixel-level visual segmentation. Matching the right architecture to the task is key.

LLMs (Large Language Models) process text token-by-token and are the most versatile architecture. Use them for: text generation, reasoning, code synthesis, summarization, translation, and Q&A. Examples: GPT-4, LLaMA 3, Claude 3, Gemini, Mixtral.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are the foundation of modern AI text systems. They excel at creative writing, complex reasoning, code generation, and conversation. They work by predicting the next token in a sequence, giving them remarkable generative power.

LCMs (Large Concept Models) are Meta's newer approach that encodes entire sentences as 'concepts' in SONAR embedding space. Unlike LLMs that work token-by-token, LCMs operate at the concept level, making them more language-agnostic and better at abstract semantic reasoning.

VLMs (Vision-Language Models) combine visual and textual understanding. Use them for: image captioning, visual QA, chart reading, OCR, video description, and document parsing. Examples: GPT-4o, LLaVA, Gemini Vision, CLIP, BLIP-2, Qwen-VL.

Vision-Language Models bridge the gap between what AI sees and what it says. They process both image patches and text tokens simultaneously, making them ideal for any task that requires understanding the content of images.

SLMs (Small Language Models) are compact, efficient models optimized for edge devices. Use them when you need: on-device AI, low latency, offline inference, mobile apps, or privacy-preserving local processing. Examples: Phi-3-mini, Gemma 2B, TinyLlama, Mistral 7B.

MoE (Mixture of Experts) models activate only the relevant expert sub-networks per query, not the full model. This makes them dramatically more compute-efficient while maintaining high performance. Use for high-throughput serving and multi-task workloads. Examples: Mixtral 8x7B, Switch Transformer, DeepSeek-MoE.

MLMs (Masked Language Models) are bidirectional — they understand context from both left and right simultaneously. They excel at NLU tasks: text classification, named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and semantic search. Examples: BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, ELECTRA, XLM-R. They are less suitable for open-ended text generation.

LAMs (Large Action Models) bridge AI understanding with real-world action. They can browse the web, use APIs, control software, and execute multi-step workflows autonomously. Use them for task automation, agentic systems, and computer use scenarios. Examples: Claude (computer use), GPT-4 with tools, ACT-1.

SAMs (Segment Anything Models) provide pixel-level visual segmentation for any image without task-specific training. Use them for: object segmentation, medical imaging analysis, video tracking, robotics perception, and dataset annotation. Examples: SAM (Meta), SAM 2, FastSAM, MobileSAM, EfficientSAM.

To pick the right architecture: Use LLM for general text/code/reasoning. Use VLM for image or video understanding. Use SLM for edge/mobile/offline needs. Use MLM for classification or NLU. Use MoE for high-efficiency large-scale inference. Use LCM for language-agnostic concept reasoning. Use LAM for autonomous agents and task automation. Use SAM for image/video segmentation.

Architecture selection guide: Text generation → LLM. Image understanding → VLM. On-device/mobile → SLM. Classification/NLU → MLM. Cost-efficient large scale → MoE. Cross-lingual semantic tasks → LCM. Autonomous task execution → LAM. Image/video segmentation → SAM.
